We aim to determine the column density ratios of six O-COMs with respect to methanol () in a sample of 14 high-mass protostellar sources to investigate their origin through ice and/or gas-phase chemistry.

The column density ratios of the six selected O-COMs with respect to methanol show no clear difference between the five low-mass studied previously and the 14 high-mass protostellar objects observed with ALMA, suggesting that these species are mainly formed under similar conditions.
In particular, the ratios of DME/MF and /GA are quite consistently around 1, while others show larger scatter.

Although the CoCCoA sources have different morphologies and brightness in their continuum and methanol emission, the O-COM ratios with respect to methanol have very similar values in the high-mass and low-mass samples.

The column density ratios of the six selected O-COMs with respect to methanol show no clear difference between the five low-mass studied previously and the 14 high-mass protostellar objects observed with ALMA, suggesting that these species are mainly formed under similar conditions.

DME and MF have the highest and most constant ratios within one order of magnitude, while the other four species have lower ratios and exhibit larger scatter by 1–2 orders of magnitude. The ratio between DME and MF is close to 1, which agrees well with previous observational findings.

DME and MF show smaller scatter in their ratios with respect to methanol than , , GA, and EG. This may hint at some chemical links among DME, MF, and methanol, such as having the same precursor (e.g., ) in their formation routes.
Current simulations and experiments can reproduce most observational trends with a few exceptions, for example, they tend to overestimate the abundance of ethanol and GA with respect to methanol.

However, despite the large scatter in the observed abundance ratios of GA and EG, it is obvious that EG is overall more abundant than GA in observations, while the G22 models give the opposite results.

Comparison with the state-of-the-art models shows consistency for some O-COMs such as DME and MF. The differences between models and observations may result from less constrained gas-phase chemistry ( and ) and the different emitting areas under limited spatial resolutions (GA and EG).

We emphasize the importance of detecting optically thin lines of minor isotopologues of methanol, which requires higher sensitivity, in order to better constrain the column density of methanol and hence the ratios with respect to other O-COMs.

If both $^{13}$ and CH$_3^{18}$OH are optically thin, we can expect their column density ratio to be 7–8. However, our fitting results show a ratio of 2–5, which indicates that $^{13}$ is also (marginally) optically thick. Therefore, only CH$_3^{18}$OH is used to calculate the column density of methanol.

However, in some bright sources such as G34.30+0.20 (Fig. [1](#fig:maps)), the methanol emission shows a ring shape around the continuum peak, which is likely due to the high optical depth of dust (cite: DeSiomone2020; MvG2022). In this case, we picked the brightest pixel on the ring to extract the spectra.

For the two bright sources G34.41+0.24 and G23.21-0.37, the methanol emission peaks at the same location as the continuum, but the spectrum extracted from the central pixel has too much line blending, so we deliberately chose a pixel offset from the actual peak ($\sim$9 pixels offset for G34.41 and $\sim$3 pixels offset for G23.21).

The upper tuning covers about 70% of the COM lines found in both tunings (not including ), while the lower one is more abundant in strong lines of and CH$_3$CN, which are not directly relevant to our project. Therefore, we consider our results to be robust using only the data in the upper tuning.

This is likely the case in the CoCCoA observations since the moment 0 maps of selected O-COMs given in Fig. [7](#fig:OCOM_mom0_G19.88) show that the emission of these molecules are barely or not spatially resolved.
For species such as CH$_3^{18}$OH, GA, and $g$-EG, there are few unblended lines covering a wide range of $E_\mathrm{up}$.

As a solution, $T_\mathrm{ex}$ was fixed to that of MF, which has the most identified transitions and therefore the best constraint on $T_\mathrm{ex}$, and only $N$ was fitted and estimated for uncertainties.

However, the sample here is too small to draw any robust conclusion. A larger sample of sources at different evolutionary stages are needed to study the chemical inheritance throughout star formation.
